statement: In an open Jackson network of $J$ single-server queues (Poisson arrivals at rates $\lambda_i$, exponential service at rates $\mu_i$, Markov routing $r_{ij}$), let $\alpha$ solve the traffic equations and put $\rho_i = \alpha_i/\mu_i$. If $0<\rho_i<1$ for every $i$, the queue-length [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) has the unique stationary distribution $\pi(n)=\prod_i(1-\rho_i)\rho_i^{n_i}$.

hypotheses.text: External arrivals to queue $i$ form a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) of rate $\lambda_i$, services at queue $i$ are exponential with rate $\mu_i$, and a served job goes to queue $j$ with probability $r_{ij}$ or leaves with probability $r_{i0}$.
The network is open: every job leaves eventually, so $I-R$ is invertible and $\alpha_i=\lambda_i+\sum_j\alpha_j r_{ji}$ has a unique solution.
The traffic rates satisfy $0<\rho_i<1$ for every queue $i$.

conclusion: The queue-length process has exactly one stationary distribution, and it is $\pi(n)=\prod_i(1-\rho_i)\rho_i^{n_i}$, so the queue lengths are independent geometric variables at equilibrium.

proofs.name: Guess the reversed process
proofs.slogan: Verify the product form against a guessed time-reversed chain, which shows that it satisfies global balance.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Every queue is assumed to receive traffic ($\alpha_i>0$), so that the chain is irreducible and the reversed rates are defined.

roles.why: Gives the transition rates of the chain on $\mathbb{N}^J$ that the proof reverses.
Gives the unique traffic rates $\alpha$ and lets every job leave, so the chain reaches the empty state.
The bound $\rho_i<1$ makes $\pi$ a probability distribution, and $\rho_i>0$ keeps the reversed rates finite.

steps.slogan: Write the transition rates of the queue-length chain on $\mathbb{N}^J$.
steps.detail: From $n$ the chain goes to $n+e_i$ at rate $\lambda_i$, and, when $n_i>0$, to $n-e_i+e_j$ at rate $\mu_i r_{ij}$ and to $n-e_i$ at rate $\mu_i r_{i0}$. The total rate $q(n)=\sum_i\lambda_i+\sum_{n_i>0}\mu_i$ is bounded, so the chain does not explode. It is irreducible, because jobs leave and $\alpha_i>0$ lets every queue fill from $0$.

steps.slogan: Sum the traffic equations to link total arrivals and total departures.
steps.detail: Summing $\alpha_i=\lambda_i+\sum_j\alpha_j r_{ji}$ over $i$ gives $\sum_i\lambda_i=\sum_j\alpha_j r_{j0}$. Put $r^*_{ji}=\alpha_i r_{ij}/\alpha_j$ and $r^*_{j0}=\lambda_j/\alpha_j$. The traffic equations say that $r^*_{j0}+\sum_i r^*_{ji}=1$ for every $j$.

steps.slogan: Define the reversed rates $q^*(m,n)=\pi(n)q(n,m)/\pi(m)$ and compute them.
steps.detail: With $\pi(n)=\prod_i(1-\rho_i)\rho_i^{n_i}$ and $\rho_i=\alpha_i/\mu_i$, the reversed rates are $q^*(m,m+e_i)=\alpha_i r_{i0}$, $q^*(m,m-e_j)=\mu_j r^*_{j0}$ and $q^*(m,m-e_j+e_i)=\mu_j r^*_{ji}$, each of the last two when $m_j>0$. For example, $\pi(m+e_i)\mu_i r_{i0}/\pi(m)=\rho_i\mu_i r_{i0}=\alpha_i r_{i0}$.

steps.slogan: Check that forward and reversed total exit rates agree at every state.
steps.detail: The reversed exit rate of $m$ is $\sum_i\alpha_i r_{i0}+\sum_{m_j>0}\mu_j(r^*_{j0}+\sum_i r^*_{ji})$. By the traffic step this equals $\sum_i\lambda_i+\sum_{m_j>0}\mu_j=q(m)$.

steps.slogan: Sum the reversal identity over all states to get global balance.
steps.detail: Fix $m$. Since $\pi(n)q(n,m)=\pi(m)q^*(m,n)$, summing over $n$ gives $\sum_n\pi(n)q(n,m)=\pi(m)\sum_n q^*(m,n)=\pi(m)q(m)$. These are the global balance equations, so $\pi$ is a stationary measure.

steps.slogan: Normalize $\pi$ and use irreducibility to prove that it is the only stationary distribution.
steps.detail: Because $\rho_i<1$, $\sum_n\pi(n)=\prod_i\sum_{k\ge0}(1-\rho_i)\rho_i^k=1$. An irreducible non-explosive chain with a stationary distribution is [positive recurrent](c:positive-recurrence), and its stationary distribution is unique.

concepts.c:markov-chain: The queue-length vector is a Markov chain whose stationary law is sought.
concepts.c:poisson-process: Poisson arrivals make the queue lengths a Markov chain.
concepts.c:positive-recurrence: A stationary distribution of an irreducible chain makes it positive recurrent and fixes it.

source.note: The reversed-process proof of Kelly, Reversibility and Stochastic Networks (Wiley, 1979), chapter 2; the theorem is J. R. Jackson, Jobshop-like queueing systems, Management Science 10 (1963).

statement: Let $S$ be a [local ring](c:local-ring) and an $R$-algebra with [residue field](c:residue-field) $k$, and let $0\to I\to P\to S\to 0$ be a presentation with $P$ [formally smooth](c:formal-smoothness) over $R$, $\Omega_{P/R}$ finite free over $P$ and $I$ finitely generated. Then $S$ is formally smooth over $R$ if and only if $k\otimes I/I^2\to k\otimes\Omega_{P/R}$ is injective.

hypotheses.text: The ring $S$ is a [local ring](c:local-ring) and an $R$-algebra, with [residue field](c:residue-field) $k$.
A surjective $R$-algebra map $P\to S$ has kernel $I$, and $P$ is [formally smooth](c:formal-smoothness) over $R$.
The module $\Omega_{P/R}$ of [Kähler differentials](c:kahler-differential) is finite free over $P$.
The ideal $I$ is finitely generated.

conclusion: $S$ is formally smooth over $R$ if and only if the map $k\otimes_S I/I^2\to k\otimes_P\Omega_{P/R}$ is injective.

formal.difference: The declaration states the criterion for an extension $P$ of $S$ over $R$, with the map $k\otimes P.\mathrm{cotangentComplex}$. The classical rank-of-the-Jacobian-matrix form follows when $P$ is a polynomial ring of finite type.

proofs.name: Split injection over a local ring
proofs.slogan: Formal smoothness is a splitting of the conormal map, and over a local ring a splitting is tested after tensoring with the residue field.
proofs.scope: The whole criterion, in the form of the mathlib declaration. The proof compares the two statements through split injectivity of the conormal map $I/I^2\to S\otimes_P\Omega_{P/R}$.

roles.why: Over a local ring, Nakayama's lemma turns a splitting into an injectivity test on the residue field.
A formally smooth $P$ with a presentation of $S$ makes smoothness of $S$ equivalent to a splitting of the conormal map.
A finite free target makes the test over the local ring applicable.
A finitely generated $I$ makes $I/I^2$ a finite module over $S$.

steps.slogan: Express formal smoothness of $S$ as a left inverse of the conormal map.
steps.detail: Since $P$ is [formally smooth](c:formal-smoothness), $S$ is formally smooth over $R$ if and only if the $S$-linear map $I/I^2\to S\otimes_P\Omega_{P/R}$ has a left inverse (Stacks 031I). This is the criterion that the conormal sequence $0\to I/I^2\to S\otimes_P\Omega_{P/R}\to\Omega_{S/R}\to0$ is split exact if and only if $S$ is formally smooth.

steps.slogan: Show that $I/I^2$ is a finite module over $S$.
steps.detail: If $I$ is generated by $g_1,\dots,g_r$, then $I/I^2$ is generated by their classes as a $P$-module. It is killed by $I$, so it is a finitely generated module over $S=P/I$.

steps.slogan: Show that $S\otimes_P\Omega_{P/R}$ is a finite [free module](c:free-module) over $S$.
steps.detail: The module $\Omega_{P/R}$ is finite free over $P$, and base change along $P\to S$ keeps a finite free module finite free.

steps.slogan: Test splitting of a map from a finite module to a finite free module over a local ring.
steps.detail: Let $l\colon M\to N$ with $M$ finite and $N$ finite free over a local ring. If $k\otimes l$ is injective, Nakayama's lemma shows that $N/l(M)$ is free, so $l(M)$ is a direct summand of $N$ and $l$ splits. Conversely a left inverse of $l$ tensors to a left inverse of $k\otimes l$.

steps.slogan: Combine the steps to compare formal smoothness with injectivity after tensoring.
steps.detail: Take $l$ to be the conormal map. Then $S$ is formally smooth if and only if $l$ splits, if and only if $k\otimes l$ is injective.

concepts.c:local-ring: Splitting is tested on the residue field only because $S$ is local.
concepts.c:residue-field: The residue field $k$ carries the injectivity test.
concepts.c:formal-smoothness: Smoothness of $P$ and of $S$ is what the criterion links.
concepts.c:kahler-differential: The target of the conormal map is built from the Kähler differentials of $P$.
concepts.c:free-module: A finite free target is needed to test a splitting on the residue field.

source.note: mathlib rewrites with Algebra.Extension.formallySmooth_iff_split_injection and IsLocalRing.split_injective_iff_lTensor_residueField_injective, after showing the cotangent module is finite.

statement: Let $H$ be a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) of finite dimension $d\ge3$. No map $v$ from the [projection operators](c:projection-operator) of $H$ to $\{0,1\}$ has $v(I)=1$ and $v(P+Q)=v(P)+v(Q)$ for all projections with $PQ=0$.

hypotheses.text: The [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ has finite dimension $d\ge3$.

conclusion: No noncontextual value assignment exists: every map $v$ with $v(I)=1$ and additive on orthogonal projections takes a value outside $\{0,1\}$ on some projection.

proofs.name: Finite configuration of rays
proofs.slogan: Reduce an assignment to a 0-1 labelling of rays in three dimensions, then refute every labelling of a finite configuration.
proofs.scope: Dimensions $d\ge3$, real or complex scalars. The outline rests on the published finite configuration of rays and its case analysis; the reduction steps are written out.

roles.why: Dimension at least 3 gives a three-dimensional subspace that holds the configuration of rays.

steps.slogan: Show that exactly one vector of every [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) has value 1.
steps.detail: Suppose that $v$ exists. For an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_d$, the projections $P_{e_k}$ are orthogonal with sum $I$, so $\sum_k v(P_{e_k})=v(I)=1$. Each value is $0$ or $1$, so exactly one is $1$.

steps.slogan: Restrict $v$ to a three-dimensional subspace where it still labels rays.
steps.detail: By step 1 some unit vector $u$ has $v(P_u)=1$. For a subspace $V\ni u$ of dimension 3, $P_V=P_u+P_{V\ominus u}$ gives $v(P_V)=1$. So every orthonormal triple $a,b,c$ of $V$ has $v(P_a)+v(P_b)+v(P_c)=1$.

steps.slogan: Fix a finite set of rays in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that contains many orthonormal triples.
steps.detail: Kochen and Specker use 117 rays; Peres later gave a version with 33 rays and 16 triples. The rays are chosen so that each triple is a set of mutually orthogonal rays and rays are shared between triples.

steps.slogan: Show that no 0-1 labelling of the rays has exactly one 1 in every triple.
steps.detail: Kochen and Specker first prove, with a small orthogonality graph, that value 1 on a ray forces value 1 on another ray at a fixed angle. They chain this implication through the configuration until two orthogonal rays both have value 1, which breaks the rule of step 2.

steps.slogan: Conclude that no assignment $v$ exists in dimension 3 or more.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give a contradiction from the existence of $v$, so no such $v$ exists. The restriction to $V$ in step 2 is the only place where $d>3$ differs from $d=3$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The assignment is defined on the projections of the Hilbert space.
concepts.c:projection-operator: Values are assigned to projection operators and must add on orthogonal ones.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: An orthonormal basis splits $I$ into orthogonal projections that add to 1.

source.ref: S. Kochen and E. P. Specker, The problem of hidden variables in quantum mechanics, Journal of Mathematics and Mechanics 17 (1967), 59-87
source.note: Reduction as in the original paper. A. Peres, Two simple proofs of the Kochen-Specker theorem, Journal of Physics A 24 (1991), L175, gives the 33-ray version.

statement: Let $x\ne0$ be an [algebraic integer](c:algebraic-integer) of a [number field](c:number-field) $K$ such that every conjugate $\varphi(x)$, for $\varphi\colon K\to\mathbb{C}$, has absolute value at most 1. Then $x$ is a [root of unity](c:root-of-unity).

hypotheses.text: The element $x$ of the [number field](c:number-field) $K$ is an [algebraic integer](c:algebraic-integer).
The element $x$ is not zero.
Every embedding $\varphi\colon K\to\mathbb{C}$ has $|\varphi(x)|\le1$.

formal.difference: The declaration tests all embeddings of $K$ into an algebraically closed normed field $A$, for example $\mathbb{C}$. The Wikipedia source of this record describes Kronecker's approximation theorem, a different result, and this proof follows the declaration.

proofs.name: Finitely many bounded integers
proofs.slogan: Only finitely many algebraic integers of $K$ have all conjugates in the unit disk, so two powers of $x$ coincide.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The case $x=0$ is excluded because $0$ is not a root of unity.

roles.why: Integrality makes every power integral and gives a monic integer minimal polynomial.
The bound on conjugates bounds the roots of the minimal polynomial, hence its coefficients.
A nonzero element can be cancelled in the field $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that every power of $x$ is an integer with conjugates in the unit disk.
steps.detail: Algebraic integers form a ring, so $x^m$ is an algebraic integer. For every embedding $\varphi$, $|\varphi(x^m)|=|\varphi(x)|^m\le1$.

steps.slogan: Bound the coefficients of the minimal polynomial of such an integer.
steps.detail: Let $y$ be an algebraic integer of $K$ with all $|\varphi(y)|\le1$ and let $d=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$. Its minimal polynomial is monic with integer coefficients, degree at most $d$, and roots $\varphi(y)$. By Vieta's formulas, each coefficient is at most $\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ in absolute value.

steps.slogan: Show that only finitely many such integers exist in $K$.
steps.detail: Only finitely many monic integer polynomials of degree at most $d$ have coefficients in $[-C,C]$, and each has at most $d$ roots. So the set $F$ of algebraic integers of $K$ with all conjugates in the unit disk is finite.

steps.slogan: Find two equal powers of $x$ by the pigeonhole principle.
steps.detail: By step 1 all the infinitely many powers $x^0,x^1,x^2,\dots$ lie in the finite set $F$. So $x^a=x^b$ for some $a>b\ge0$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the common factor to get a power of $x$ equal to 1.
steps.detail: From $x^b(x^{a-b}-1)=0$ in the field $K$ and $x\ne0$, we get $x^{a-b}=1$ with $a-b\ge1$.

concepts.c:algebraic-integer: Algebraic integers are closed under powers and have integer minimal polynomials.
concepts.c:number-field: A number field has finitely many embeddings and a fixed degree $d$.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: A power of $x$ equal to 1 is what the proof produces.

source.note: mathlib uses NumberField.Embeddings.finite_of_norm_le (bounded minimal-polynomial coefficients) and Set.Infinite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_mapsTo on the powers of x.

statement: Let $R$ be a [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring) [local ring](c:local-ring) and $I$ a proper [ideal](c:ideal). Then $\bigcap_{n\ge0}I^n=0$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a commutative [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring).
The ring $R$ is a [local ring](c:local-ring) with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.
The [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ is proper: $I\ne R$.

conclusion: The intersection $\bigcap_{n\ge0}I^n$ of all powers of $I$ is the zero ideal.

proofs.name: Artin-Rees and Nakayama
proofs.slogan: Show that the intersection $N$ satisfies $N=IN$, find $r\in I$ with $(1-r)N=0$, and cancel the unit $1-r$.
proofs.scope: The ring itself as the module (mathlib proves the module version). The case $I=0$ is trivial.

roles.why: Noetherianity makes $N$ finitely generated and gives the Artin-Rees lemma.
In a local ring every element outside $\mathfrak m$ is a unit.
A proper ideal lies in $\mathfrak m$, so $1-r$ is a unit for $r\in I$.

steps.slogan: Name the intersection $N$ and show that it is a finitely generated ideal.
steps.detail: Put $N=\bigcap_n I^n$. Then $N$ is an ideal of the [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring) $R$, so it is finitely generated.

steps.slogan: Show $N=IN$ with the Artin-Rees lemma.
steps.detail: Artin-Rees gives $k$ with $I^{n}\cap N=I^{n-k}(I^k\cap N)$ for $n\ge k$. Here $N\subseteq I^n$ for every $n$, so $I^{k+1}\cap N=N$ and $N=I(I^k\cap N)\subseteq IN\subseteq N$.

steps.slogan: Find $r\in I$ with $rx=x$ for all $x\in N$ by the determinant trick.
steps.detail: The ideal $N$ is finitely generated and $N=IN$. The determinant (Cayley-Hamilton) argument behind Nakayama's lemma gives $r\in I$ with $(1-r)N=0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $1-r$ is a unit of the [local ring](c:local-ring) $R$.
steps.detail: A proper ideal lies in the unique [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$, so $r\in\mathfrak m$. Then $1-r\notin\mathfrak m$, so $1-r$ is a unit.

steps.slogan: Cancel the unit $1-r$ to get $N=0$.
steps.detail: Take $x\in N$. Then $(1-r)x=0$, and $1-r$ is a unit of $R$, so multiplying by its inverse gives $x=0$. Hence $N=0$.

concepts.c:noetherian-ring: Noetherianity gives a finitely generated intersection and Artin-Rees.
concepts.c:local-ring: A local ring makes every element outside the maximal ideal a unit.
concepts.c:ideal: The intersection of powers of the ideal $I$ is the object studied.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: The proper ideal $I$ lies in the unique maximal ideal.

statement: Let $p$ be a [prime number](c:prime-number) and $n,k$ natural numbers. The [p-adic valuation](c:p-adic-valuation) of the [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) $\binom{n+k}{k}$ equals the number of [carries](c:carrying) when $n$ and $k$ are added in base $p$.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).
The numbers $n$ and $k$ are natural numbers (zero is allowed).

conclusion: $v_p\binom{n+k}{k}$ is the number of carries in the base-$p$ addition $n+k$.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the digit-sum form $(p-1)\,v_p\binom{n+k}{k}=s_p(k)+s_p(n)-s_p(n+k)$ and does not count carries. Step 3 below turns the digit-sum form into the carry count.

proofs.name: Legendre's formula and carries
proofs.slogan: Turn the factorial quotient into digit sums with Legendre's formula, then count the carries as the loss of digit sum.
proofs.scope: All $n,k\ge0$; if $n=0$ or $k=0$ there are no carries and the binomial coefficient is 1.

roles.why: Legendre's formula holds for a prime, and $p-1\ge1$ allows the final division.
The quotient of factorials and the digit expansions need natural numbers.

steps.slogan: Express the valuation of a factorial through the base-p [digit sum](c:digit-sum).
steps.detail: Legendre's formula gives $(p-1)\,v_p(m!)=m-s_p(m)$ for every $m\ge0$, where $s_p(m)$ is the sum of the [base-p digits](c:base-p-digits) of $m$.

steps.slogan: Write the binomial coefficient as a quotient of factorials and take valuations.
steps.detail: Since $\binom{n+k}{k}=\frac{(n+k)!}{k!\,n!}$ and $v_p$ turns products into sums, $v_p\binom{n+k}{k}=v_p((n+k)!)-v_p(k!)-v_p(n!)$. Multiply by $p-1$ and insert step 1: $(p-1)v_p\binom{n+k}{k}=s_p(n)+s_p(k)-s_p(n+k)$, because the terms $n+k$, $k$ and $n$ cancel.

steps.slogan: Show that each carry lowers the digit sum by $p-1$.
steps.detail: Let $c_0=0$ and let $c_{i+1}\in\{0,1\}$ be the carry out of position $i$, so that $n_i+k_i+c_i=m_i+p\,c_{i+1}$, with $m_i$ the digits of $n+k$. Summing over all $i$ and using $\sum_i c_i=\sum_i c_{i+1}=C$ gives $s_p(n)+s_p(k)-s_p(n+k)=(p-1)C$, with $C$ the number of carries.

steps.slogan: Divide by $p-1$ to equate the valuation with the carry count.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 both express $s_p(n)+s_p(k)-s_p(n+k)$, so $(p-1)v_p\binom{n+k}{k}=(p-1)C$. Since $p-1\ge1$, we divide and get $v_p\binom{n+k}{k}=C$.

concepts.c:prime-number: Legendre's formula and the valuation $v_p$ need a prime $p$.
concepts.c:p-adic-valuation: The valuation $v_p$ is the quantity counted by the carries.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The coefficient $\binom{n+k}{k}$ is the quotient whose valuation is studied.
concepts.c:carrying: Each carry in the addition lowers the digit sum by $p-1$.
concepts.c:digit-sum: Digit sums turn factorial valuations into the carry count.
concepts.c:base-p-digits: Base-$p$ digits define $s_p$ and the carries.

source.note: mathlib rewrites the binomial coefficient as a factorial quotient (Nat.choose_eq_factorial_div_factorial) and applies sub_one_mul_padicValNat_factorial (Legendre) to each factorial.

statement: If a conservative scheme (consistent Lipschitz numerical flux, fixed ratio $\Delta t/\Delta x$) for the [conservation law](c:conservation-law) $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ has bounded numerical solutions that converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to $u$, with initial data converging to $u_0$, then $u$ is a [weak solution](c:weak-solution).

hypotheses.text: The scheme is conservative, in [finite volume](c:finite-volume-method) form: $U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\lambda(F^n_{j+1/2}-F^n_{j-1/2})$ with $F^n_{j+1/2}=F(U^n_{j-p+1},\dots,U^n_{j+q})$ and $\lambda=\Delta t/\Delta x$ fixed.
The numerical flux $F$ is [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) on bounded sets and consistent: $F(v,\dots,v)=f(v)$.

Along a sequence $\Delta x\to0$ the piecewise constant solutions $u_{\Delta x}$ satisfy $|u_{\Delta x}|\le M$, converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to $u$, and $u_{\Delta x}(\cdot,0)\to u_0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

proofs.name: Summation by parts
proofs.slogan: Multiply the scheme by a test function, sum by parts to move differences onto it, and pass to the limit.
proofs.scope: Systems $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$ with $f$ locally Lipschitz; no entropy condition is claimed, only the weak form. The limit exists by hypothesis, and the proof does not use total variation bounds.

roles.why: The conservative form makes the flux terms telescope under summation by parts.
Consistency and the Lipschitz bound send the numerical flux to $f(u)$ in the limit.
Bounded $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence passes the limit through the integrals, and the initial data give the initial term.

steps.slogan: Multiply the scheme by a test function and sum over the grid.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi\in C_c^1$, $x_j=j\Delta x$, $t_n=n\Delta t$ and $\varphi_j^n=\varphi(x_j,t_n)$. Multiplying the scheme by $\varphi_j^n$ and summing over $j$ and $n\ge0$ gives $\sum\varphi_j^n(U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n)=-\lambda\sum\varphi_j^n(F^n_{j+1/2}-F^n_{j-1/2})$. The sums are finite because $\varphi$ has compact support.

steps.slogan: Sum by parts in time and in space to move the differences onto $\varphi$.
steps.detail: After multiplying by $\Delta x$, the identity reads $\Delta x\Delta t\sum_{n\ge1,j}U_j^n\frac{\varphi_j^n-\varphi_j^{n-1}}{\Delta t}+\Delta x\Delta t\sum_{n\ge0,j}F^n_{j+1/2}\frac{\varphi^n_{j+1}-\varphi^n_j}{\Delta x}+\Delta x\sum_jU_j^0\varphi_j^0=0$. No boundary terms remain, because $\varphi$ vanishes for large $|x|$ and large $t$.

steps.slogan: Write the three sums as integrals of the piecewise constant solution.
steps.detail: The sums equal $\iint u_{\Delta x}D_t\varphi$, $\iint F(\text{shifts of }u_{\Delta x})D_x\varphi$ and $\int u_{\Delta x}(x,0)\varphi(x,0)\,dx$, up to errors that tend to $0$. Here $D_t\varphi$ and $D_x\varphi$ are difference quotients, which converge uniformly to $\varphi_t$ and $\varphi_x$ with supports in one compact set.

steps.slogan: Show that the numerical flux values converge to $f(u)$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
steps.detail: Translation is continuous in $L^1$, so the values of $u_{\Delta x}$ shifted by $i\Delta x$ also converge to $u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. On $|v|\le M$, consistency and the Lipschitz constant $L$ of $F$ give $|F(v_{-p+1},\dots,v_q)-f(v_0)|\le L\max_i|v_i-v_0|$, and $f(v)=F(v,\dots,v)$ is Lipschitz too. So both the flux values and $f(u_{\Delta x})$ converge to $f(u)$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in the integral identity to get the weak form.
steps.detail: A bounded sequence that converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, integrated against uniformly convergent compactly supported functions, converges to the limit integral. So $\iint(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x)\,dx\,dt+\int u_0\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0$ for every $\varphi$, and $u$ is a [weak solution](c:weak-solution).

concepts.c:conservation-law: The limit is claimed to solve the conservation law in the weak sense.
concepts.c:weak-solution: The integral identity against test functions defines the weak solution.
concepts.c:finite-volume-method: Conservative form means flux differences between cells, which telescope.
concepts.c:lipschitz-continuous-function: A Lipschitz flux turns closeness of the values into closeness of the fluxes.
concepts.c:test-function: Test functions let the differences move onto smooth functions.

source.note: The proof of P. D. Lax and B. Wendroff, Systems of conservation laws, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 13 (1960), 217-237, as presented in LeVeque, Numerical Methods for Conservation Laws (Birkhauser, 1992), chapter 12.

statement: The [Lazard ring](c:lazard-ring) $L$ of the universal one-dimensional [formal group law](c:formal-group-law) is a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $\mathbb{Z}[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ with one generator $x_i$ in each degree $2i$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $L$ carries the [universal](c:universal-property) commutative one-dimensional formal group law $F_L$: every such law over a ring $A$ is the image of $F_L$ under a unique ring map $L\to A$.

proofs.name: Cocycle lemma and rank count
proofs.slogan: Build the universal law, show by the symmetric cocycle lemma that one generator per degree suffices, and compare ranks over the rationals.
proofs.scope: An outline of Lazard's proof: the cocycle lemma and the rational logarithm are cited, not reproved. Both rings are graded with $|x_i|=2i$.

roles.why: The universal property defines $L$ and the law $F_L$ whose coefficients generate it.

steps.slogan: Build the universal formal group law over a graded ring $L$.
steps.detail: Let $L=\mathbb{Z}[a_{ij}]/J$, where $J$ imposes $F(x,0)=x$, commutativity and associativity on $F(x,y)=x+y+\sum a_{ij}x^iy^j$. Giving $a_{ij}$ degree $2(i+j-1)$ grades $L$ and makes $F_L$ homogeneous. By construction $L$ has the universal property.

steps.slogan: Compute $L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ through the logarithm.
steps.detail: Over a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra every formal group law is $\exp(\log x+\log y)$ for a unique logarithm $\log x=x+\sum_{i\ge1}m_ix^{i+1}$. So $L\otimes\mathbb{Q}\cong\mathbb{Q}[m_1,m_2,\dots]$ with $m_i$ in degree $2i$.

steps.slogan: Classify the homogeneous symmetric 2-cocycles of each degree.
steps.detail: Lazard's lemma: every homogeneous symmetric 2-[cocycle](c:cocycle) of degree $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is an integer multiple of $C_n(x,y)=\frac1{d_n}\big((x+y)^n-x^n-y^n\big)$ plus a coboundary. Here $d_n=p$ if $n=p^k$ for a prime $p$, and $d_n=1$ otherwise.

steps.slogan: Show that $L$ is generated by one element in each degree.
steps.detail: By associativity, the degree-$n$ part of $F_L$ modulo decomposables is a symmetric 2-cocycle. By step 3 it is $x_nC_n$ plus a coboundary, which a change of coordinate removes. So the indecomposables of $L$ in degree $2n$ are generated by one element $x_n$, and $\mathbb{Z}[x_1,x_2,\dots]\to L$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Compare ranks over the rationals to show that the surjection is injective.
steps.detail: The graded surjection has finitely generated pieces. After $\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ it maps $\mathbb{Q}[x_i]$ onto $L\otimes\mathbb{Q}\cong\mathbb{Q}[m_i]$, which has the same dimension in each degree, so it is bijective. The kernel $K$ has $K\otimes\mathbb{Q}=0$ and lies in the torsion-free ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_i]$, so $K=0$.

concepts.c:lazard-ring: The Lazard ring is the ring whose structure the theorem gives.
concepts.c:formal-group-law: The universal formal group law is the object that $L$ classifies.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The conclusion is that $L$ is a polynomial ring on one generator per degree.
concepts.c:universal-property: The universal property defines $L$ and its generating coefficients.
concepts.c:cocycle: Associativity makes the leading terms of a formal group law symmetric 2-cocycles.

source.ref: M. Lazard, Sur les groupes de Lie formels a un parametre, Bulletin de la Societe Mathematique de France 83 (1955), 251-274
source.note: Modern expositions with the cocycle method: J. F. Adams, Stable Homotopy and Generalised Homology (University of Chicago Press, 1974), Part II; D. C. Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres, appendix 2.

statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be an [open cover](c:open-cover) of a [compact metric space](c:compact-metric-space) $(X,d)$. Then some $\delta>0$ has the property that every subset of $X$ of [diameter](c:diameter) less than $\delta$ lies in one member of $\mathcal U$.

hypotheses.text: The space $(X,d)$ is a [compact metric space](c:compact-metric-space).
The family $\mathcal U$ is an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$.

conclusion: There is $\delta>0$ such that every $A\subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}A<\delta$ lies in some $U\in\mathcal U$.

proofs.name: Convergent subsequence
proofs.slogan: Assume that no $\delta$ works, pick bad points, extract a convergent subsequence and trap its tails in one open set.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma. The empty space is trivial, and the empty set lies in every member of the cover.

roles.why: A compact metric space is sequentially compact, so the bad points have a convergent subsequence.
The limit point lies in an open member, which holds a ball around it.

steps.slogan: Assume that no $\delta$ works and choose a bad set for each $\delta=1/n$.
steps.detail: For every $n$ there is $A_n\subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}A_n<1/n$ that lies in no member of $\mathcal U$. Each $A_n$ is nonempty, so choose $x_n\in A_n$.

steps.slogan: Extract a convergent subsequence of the points $x_n$.
steps.detail: A [compact metric space](c:compact-metric-space) is sequentially compact, so some subsequence $x_{n_k}$ converges to a point $x\in X$.

steps.slogan: Put a ball around the limit $x$ inside one member of the cover.
steps.detail: The cover has a member $U\ni x$. Since $U$ is open, there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq U$.

steps.slogan: Show that the sets $A_{n_k}$ lie in $U$ for large $k$.
steps.detail: Take $k$ with $d(x_{n_k},x)<\varepsilon/2$ and $1/n_k<\varepsilon/2$. For $y\in A_{n_k}$, $d(y,x)\le d(y,x_{n_k})+d(x_{n_k},x)<\varepsilon$, so $A_{n_k}\subseteq U$. This contradicts the choice of $A_{n_k}$.

concepts.c:open-cover: The members of the cover are open, so one contains a ball around the limit.
concepts.c:compact-metric-space: Compactness gives the convergent subsequence of bad points.
concepts.c:diameter: Small diameter keeps the whole set $A_{n_k}$ near its chosen point.

source.note: The standard sequential-compactness argument for compact metric spaces.

proofs.name: Distance function
proofs.slogan: Average the distances to the complements of a finite subcover and take the positive minimum on the compact space.
proofs.scope: If some member of the cover equals $X$, every $\delta$ works; otherwise each complement is nonempty. The empty set lies in every member.

roles.why: Compactness gives a finite subcover and makes the continuous function attain its minimum.
The members are open, so every point has positive distance from some complement.

steps.slogan: Select a finite subcover $U_1,\dots,U_m$ of the cover.
steps.detail: Since $X$ is compact, finitely many members $U_1,\dots,U_m$ of the [open cover](c:open-cover) cover $X$. Assume that no $U_i$ equals $X$.

steps.slogan: Define $f(x)$ as the mean distance from $x$ to the complements $X\setminus U_i$.
steps.detail: Put $f(x)=\frac1m\sum_i d(x,X\setminus U_i)$. Each term is 1-Lipschitz, so $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function). Each $x$ lies in some open $U_i$, so $d(x,X\setminus U_i)>0$ and $f(x)>0$.

steps.slogan: Take the minimum $\delta>0$ of $f$ on the compact space.
steps.detail: A continuous function on a nonempty compact space attains its minimum $\delta$, and $\delta=f(x_0)>0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a set of diameter below $\delta$ lies in one $U_i$.
steps.detail: Let $\operatorname{diam}A<\delta$ and $a\in A$. The mean $f(a)$ is at least $\delta$, so its largest term is at least $\delta$: some $i$ has $d(a,X\setminus U_i)\ge\delta$. Every $y\in A$ has $d(a,y)<\delta$, so $y\in U_i$.

concepts.c:open-cover: A finite subcover of the open cover gives finitely many distance terms.
concepts.c:compact-metric-space: Compactness gives the finite subcover and the minimum of $f$.
concepts.c:diameter: Diameter below $\delta$ keeps every point of $A$ within $\delta$ of $a$.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $f$ lets it attain a minimum on the compact space.

source.note: Munkres, Topology, 2nd ed., lemma 27.5 (the Lebesgue number lemma).

statement: Let $(M,g)$ be a connected, complete [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $n\ge2$ with [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) $\mathrm{Ric}\ge(n-1)k\,g$ for a constant $k>0$. Then the [diameter](c:diameter) of $M$ is at most $\pi/\sqrt k$, $M$ is compact and the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) of $M$ is finite.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is connected and complete as a metric space.
The dimension $n$ of $M$ is at least 2.
The [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) satisfies $\mathrm{Ric}(v,v)\ge(n-1)k|v|^2$ for every tangent vector $v$, with a constant $k>0$.

conclusion: $\operatorname{diam}M\le\pi/\sqrt k$, the manifold $M$ is compact and $\pi_1(M)$ is finite.

proofs.name: Second variation of length
proofs.slogan: Join two far points by a minimizing geodesic and show by the second variation that the Ricci bound shortens it.
proofs.scope: The diameter bound is proved by contradiction. Compactness and finiteness of $\pi_1$ follow from the bound applied to $M$ and to its universal cover.

roles.why: Completeness gives minimizing geodesics (Hopf-Rinow) and makes bounded closed sets compact.
Dimension at least 2 gives at least one parallel field normal to the geodesic.
The lower Ricci bound makes the summed second variation negative.

steps.slogan: Join two points that are far apart by a minimizing unit speed [geodesic](c:geodesic).
steps.detail: Suppose $d(p,q)=\ell>\pi/\sqrt k$ for some $p,q\in M$. By the Hopf-Rinow theorem there is a minimizing unit speed geodesic $\gamma\colon[0,\ell]\to M$ from $p$ to $q$.

steps.slogan: Build variation fields along $\gamma$ from a parallel orthonormal frame.
steps.detail: Take parallel orthonormal fields $e_1,\dots,e_{n-1}$ along $\gamma$, all orthogonal to $\gamma'$. Put $V_i(t)=\sin(\pi t/\ell)\,e_i(t)$, which vanishes at both ends.

steps.slogan: Sum the second variations of length over the $n-1$ fields.
steps.detail: For a unit speed geodesic, the second variation along $V_i$ is $\int_0^\ell(|V_i'|^2-\langle R(V_i,\gamma')\gamma',V_i\rangle)\,dt$. Since $\sum_i\langle R(e_i,\gamma')\gamma',e_i\rangle=\mathrm{Ric}(\gamma',\gamma')$, the sum is $\int_0^\ell\big((n-1)\frac{\pi^2}{\ell^2}\cos^2\frac{\pi t}{\ell}-\sin^2\frac{\pi t}{\ell}\,\mathrm{Ric}(\gamma',\gamma')\big)dt$.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum with the Ricci lower bound to get a negative number.
steps.detail: With $\mathrm{Ric}(\gamma',\gamma')\ge(n-1)k$, the sum is at most $(n-1)\frac{\ell}{2}\big(\frac{\pi^2}{\ell^2}-k\big)$. This is negative because $\ell>\pi/\sqrt k$.

steps.slogan: Contradict minimality: some variation of $\gamma$ is shorter.
steps.detail: Some $V_i$ has negative second variation, so nearby curves from $p$ to $q$ are shorter than $\gamma$. This contradicts minimality of $\gamma$, so $\operatorname{diam}M\le\pi/\sqrt k$.

steps.slogan: Deduce compactness of $M$ and finiteness of $\pi_1(M)$ from the diameter bound.
steps.detail: A complete space of finite diameter is a closed ball, which is compact by Hopf-Rinow. The universal [covering space](c:covering-space) with the lifted metric is complete with the same Ricci bound, so it is compact too. Its fibres over $M$ are closed and discrete, hence finite, and they are in bijection with $\pi_1(M)$.

concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: The theorem is a statement about complete Riemannian manifolds.
concepts.c:ricci-curvature: The Ricci lower bound controls the summed second variation.
concepts.c:diameter: The diameter bound is the first conclusion, proved by contradiction.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: Finiteness of the fundamental group follows from compactness of the universal cover.
concepts.c:geodesic: A minimizing geodesic between far points is the curve that is shortened.
concepts.c:covering-space: The universal cover has the same curvature bound and is compact.

source.note: The second variation proof of do Carmo, Riemannian Geometry (Birkhauser, 1992), chapter 9, the Bonnet-Myers theorem.

statement: For every natural number $n$ and real $B\ge0$, only finitely many integer [polynomials](c:polynomial) $p$ of degree at most $n$ have [Mahler measure](c:mahler-measure) $M(p)\le B$.

hypotheses.text: The degree bound $n$ is a natural number, and $p$ ranges over [polynomials](c:polynomial) in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ of degree at most $n$.
The bound $B\ge0$ is a real number and the [Mahler measure](c:mahler-measure) satisfies $M(p)\le B$.

conclusion: The set $\{p\in\mathbb{Z}[X]:\deg p\le n,\ M(p)\le B\}$ is finite.

formal.difference: The declaration is the polynomial form, stated for the Mahler measure of the image in $\mathbb{C}[X]$. The classical form for algebraic numbers of bounded degree and height follows from it.

proofs.name: Coefficient box
proofs.slogan: Bound every coefficient by a binomial multiple of the Mahler measure, so the polynomials lie in a finite box of integer vectors.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge0$ and $B\ge0$; the zero polynomial has $M(0)=0$ and is a single polynomial. The Mahler measure of $p=a_d\prod_j(X-\alpha_j)$ is $M(p)=|a_d|\prod_j\max(1,|\alpha_j|)$.

roles.why: The degree bound limits the number of roots and of coefficients, and the coefficient vector has length $n+1$.
The bound on $M(p)$ bounds every coefficient.

steps.slogan: Write the Mahler measure of a nonzero polynomial through its roots.
steps.detail: For $p=a_d\prod_{j=1}^d(X-\alpha_j)$ with $a_d\ne0$, Jensen's formula gives $M(p)=|a_d|\prod_j\max(1,|\alpha_j|)$ for the [Mahler measure](c:mahler-measure).

steps.slogan: Bound each coefficient of $p$ by a binomial multiple of $M(p)$.
steps.detail: By Vieta's formulas, $a_{d-i}=\pm a_d\,e_i(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d)$ is a sum of $\binom di$ terms $\pm a_d\prod_{j\in S}\alpha_j$. Each term has absolute value at most $|a_d|\prod_j\max(1,|\alpha_j|)=M(p)$. So $|a_m|\le\binom dmM(p)\le\binom nmB$ for every $m$.

steps.slogan: Count the integer vectors in the box $|a_m|\le\binom nmB$.
steps.detail: The coefficient $a_m\in\mathbb{Z}$ has at most $2\lfloor\binom nmB\rfloor+1$ values. So the box holds at most $\prod_{m=0}^n\big(2\lfloor\binom nmB\rfloor+1\big)$ integer vectors.

steps.slogan: Embed the set of polynomials into the box by taking coefficient vectors.
steps.detail: A polynomial of degree at most $n$ is determined by $(a_0,\dots,a_n)$. By step 2 this vector lies in the box, so the set injects into a finite set and is finite.

concepts.c:polynomial: The integer polynomials of bounded degree are the objects counted.
concepts.c:mahler-measure: The Mahler measure bounds every coefficient and so gives finiteness.

source.note: mathlib bounds the coefficients (norm_coeff_le_choose_mul_mahlerMeasure) and counts the integer box (ncard_boxPoly) in Polynomial.card_mahlerMeasure.

statement: The [power set](c:power-set) of a [finite set](c:finite-set) $S$ has exactly $2^{|S|}$ elements.

hypotheses.text: The set $S$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) with $n=|S|$ elements; $n=0$ is allowed.

conclusion: $|\mathcal P(S)|=2^n$, where $\mathcal P(S)$ is the set of all subsets of $S$.

proofs.name: Induction on the size
proofs.slogan: Split the subsets of a set with one more element by whether they contain it, and double the count.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge0$. The empty set has one subset, itself.

roles.why: Finiteness lets induction on the number of elements run.

steps.slogan: Count the subsets of the empty set.
steps.detail: The empty set has exactly one subset, which is the empty set itself. This agrees with the formula, because $2^0=1$.

steps.slogan: Split the subsets of $S\cup\{a\}$ by whether they contain $a$.
steps.detail: Let $a\notin S$. A subset of $S\cup\{a\}$ either avoids $a$, and is a subset of $S$, or contains $a$, and is $A\cup\{a\}$ for a unique subset $A$ of $S$. The map $A\mapsto A\cup\{a\}$ is a [bijection](c:bijection) from $\mathcal P(S)$ onto the subsets that contain $a$.

steps.slogan: Add the two counts to get $2^{n+1}$ subsets.
steps.detail: If $S$ has $n$ elements and $2^n$ subsets, then $S\cup\{a\}$ has $2^n+2^n=2^{n+1}$ subsets, because the two classes are disjoint and have equal size.

steps.slogan: Conclude by induction on the number of elements.
steps.detail: The base case and the step give $|\mathcal P(S)|=2^{|S|}$ for every finite set $S$.

concepts.c:power-set: The power set is the collection of subsets being counted.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness lets induction on the number of elements run.
concepts.c:bijection: A bijection shows that the subsets with $a$ and without $a$ are equally many.

source.note: mathlib reduces to Multiset.card_powerset, which inducts with powerset (a ::ₘ s) = powerset s + map (cons a) (powerset s).

proofs.name: Indicator functions
proofs.slogan: Match subsets with functions from $S$ to $\{0,1\}$ and count the functions.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge0$. For $n=0$ the only function is the empty function.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the count of functions a product of $n$ factors.

steps.slogan: Send each subset $A\subseteq S$ to its indicator function $1_A\colon S\to\{0,1\}$.
steps.detail: Put $1_A(x)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $1_A(x)=0$ otherwise. This defines a map from $\mathcal P(S)$ to the functions $S\to\{0,1\}$.

steps.slogan: Show that this map is a [bijection](c:bijection) by writing its inverse.
steps.detail: The map $f\mapsto\{x\in S:f(x)=1\}$ is inverse to $A\mapsto1_A$ in both orders. So subsets of $S$ and functions $S\to\{0,1\}$ correspond one to one.

steps.slogan: Count the functions $S\to\{0,1\}$ by independent choices.
steps.detail: Each of the $n$ elements of $S$ takes one of 2 values independently, so there are $2^n$ functions. Hence $|\mathcal P(S)|=2^n$.

concepts.c:power-set: The power set is the collection of subsets being counted.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness makes the count of functions a finite product.
concepts.c:bijection: The indicator map is a bijection between subsets and 0-1 functions.

source.note: The standard bijection between subsets and characteristic functions.

statement: Revolve a plane region $R$ of [area](c:area) $A$, or a plane curve $C$ of length $L$, about a line $\ell$ of its plane that it does not cross. The [solid of revolution](c:solid-of-revolution) of $R$ has volume $2\pi\rho_RA$ and the surface of $C$ has area $2\pi\rho_CL$, where $\rho_R,\rho_C$ are the distances from $\ell$ to the [centroids](c:centroid).

hypotheses.text: The region or curve lies in one closed half-plane of the axis $\ell$.
The region $R$ is compact with piecewise smooth boundary and positive area, and $C$ is a simple piecewise $C^1$ arc of positive length.

conclusion: The volume is $V=2\pi\rho_RA$ and the surface area is $S=2\pi\rho_CL$.

proofs.name: Cylindrical coordinates
proofs.slogan: Write the volume and the surface area as integrals of the distance from the axis, and recognize the centroid in them.
proofs.scope: Both parts, with the axis as the $y$-axis. A region or curve that touches the axis is allowed; the touched set has measure zero in the swept body.

roles.why: Staying on one side makes the distance to the axis equal to $x\ge0$ and the revolution injective.
Piecewise smooth boundaries and arcs make the integrals and the area element defined.

steps.slogan: Place the axis as the $y$-axis with the figure in $x\ge0$.
steps.detail: Choose coordinates in the plane of the figure so that $\ell$ is the $y$-axis. The distance of a point to $\ell$ is its coordinate $x\ge0$.

steps.slogan: Write each centroid distance as a mean value of $x$.
steps.detail: The [centroid](c:centroid) is the mean position of the points, so $\rho_R=\frac1A\iint_Rx\,dA$ and, with arc length $s$, $\rho_C=\frac1L\int_Cx\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Compute the volume of the [solid of revolution](c:solid-of-revolution) in cylindrical coordinates.
steps.detail: The solid is the image of $\{(x,y,\theta):(x,y)\in R,\ 0\le\theta<2\pi\}$ under $(x,y,\theta)\mapsto(x\cos\theta,y,x\sin\theta)$, which is injective off a null set because $x\ge0$. The Jacobian is $x$, so $V=\iint_R\int_0^{2\pi}x\,d\theta\,dA=2\pi\iint_Rx\,dA$.

steps.slogan: Compute the area of the swept surface from its area element.
steps.detail: Parametrize $C$ by arc length, $s\mapsto(x(s),y(s))$, and the surface by $(s,\theta)\mapsto(x\cos\theta,y,x\sin\theta)$. The two partial derivatives are orthogonal with lengths $1$ and $x$, so the area element is $x\,ds\,d\theta$ and $S=2\pi\int_Cx\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the centroid formulas to get both results.
steps.detail: By the centroid step, $\iint_Rx\,dA=\rho_RA$ and $\int_Cx\,ds=\rho_CL$. Substituting into the volume and surface formulas gives $V=2\pi\rho_RA$ and $S=2\pi\rho_CL$.

concepts.c:area: The area $A$ of the region is the factor in the volume formula.
concepts.c:solid-of-revolution: The swept solid is the body whose volume the theorem gives.
concepts.c:centroid: The centroid is the mean of $x$, which the integrals contain.

source.note: The standard calculus proof by cylindrical coordinates; the theorem is due to Pappus of Alexandria and was restated by Guldin.

statement: A nonconstant [entire function](c:entire-function) omits at most one complex value (little Picard). Near an [essential singularity](c:essential-singularity), a holomorphic function takes every complex value infinitely often, with at most one exception (great Picard).

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $\mathbb{C}$ (little Picard) or on a punctured disc $0<|z|<r$ (great Picard).
In the first case $f$ is nonconstant; in the second case $f$ has an [essential singularity](c:essential-singularity) at $0$.

conclusion: In the first case $f(\mathbb{C})$ misses at most one value; in the second case, in every neighborhood of $0$, $f$ takes each value infinitely often, with at most one exception.

proofs.name: Normal families
proofs.slogan: Use the fundamental normality test for functions that omit two values, and rescale to a normal family in both cases.
proofs.scope: An outline: Montel's fundamental normality test is cited, and the two rescaling arguments are written out. Both Picard theorems follow from it.

roles.why: Holomorphy lets the rescaled functions form a normal family and lets the maximum principle apply.
Nonconstancy or the essential singularity is the property that the contradiction defeats.

steps.slogan: Cite the fundamental normality test for families that omit two values.
steps.detail: A family of holomorphic functions on a domain that all omit $0$ and $1$ is a [normal family](c:normal-family): each sequence has a subsequence that converges locally uniformly, in the spherical metric, to a holomorphic function or to $\infty$. Published proofs use Schottky's theorem or the modular function.

steps.slogan: Rescale an entire function that omits two values and force its derivative to vanish.
steps.detail: Suppose a nonconstant entire $f$ omits two values; after an affine change they are $0$ and $1$. For fixed $w$, the functions $f_k(z)=f(w+kz)$ on $|z|<1$ omit $0,1$, so a subsequence converges to a finite limit, because $f_k(0)=f(w)$ is fixed. Then $f_k'(0)=kf'(w)$ stays bounded, so $f'(w)=0$ for all $w$ and $f$ is constant, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Rescale near the singularity and bound $f$ or $1/f$ on small circles.
steps.detail: Suppose $f$ omits $0$ and $1$ on $0<|z|<r$. The functions $g_k(z)=f(z/k)$ omit $0,1$ on $\frac12<|z|<2$, so a subsequence $g_{k_j}$ converges uniformly on $|z|=1$ to a bounded holomorphic function or to $\infty$. So either $|f|\le M$ on the circles $|z|=1/k_j$, or $|f|\ge1$ on them for large $j$.

steps.slogan: Spread the bound over a punctured neighborhood by the maximum modulus principle.
steps.detail: Apply the maximum modulus principle to $f$, or to $1/f$ in the second case, on the annuli between consecutive circles $|z|=1/k_j$. Then $f$ or $1/f$ is bounded near $0$, so the singularity is removable or a pole by Riemann's theorem. This contradicts an essential singularity.

steps.slogan: Turn finitely many takings of two values into two omitted values.
steps.detail: Let $f$ have an essential singularity at $0$, and suppose two values $b\ne c$ are each taken only finitely often near $0$. In a smaller punctured disc $f$ omits both, and an affine change makes them $0$ and $1$, which the previous step excludes. So at most one value is exceptional.

steps.slogan: Combine the entire case and the essential singularity case.
steps.detail: Step 2 shows that a nonconstant entire function omits at most one value. Step 5 shows that near an essential singularity every value but at most one is taken infinitely often.

concepts.c:entire-function: Little Picard is a statement about nonconstant entire functions.
concepts.c:essential-singularity: Great Picard describes the values near an essential singularity.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives normal families and the maximum principle.
concepts.c:normal-family: Normality of the rescaled functions is the engine of both parts.

source.ref: J. B. Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, 2nd edition, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 11, Springer, 1978, chapter XII (The Range of an Analytic Function)
source.note: Chapter XII proves the little and the great Picard theorems from Montel's normality test; the rescaling steps follow that chapter.

statement: For a [simple polygon](c:simple-polygon) with vertices at [lattice points](c:lattice-point), the [area](c:area) is $A=I+\frac B2-1$, where $I$ and $B$ count the lattice points in the interior and on the boundary.

hypotheses.text: The polygon $P$ is [simple](c:simple-polygon): its boundary is a closed curve without self-intersections.
Every vertex of $P$ is a [lattice point](c:lattice-point), a point of $\mathbb{Z}^2$.

proofs.name: Triangulation and parallelograms
proofs.slogan: Show that the defect is additive, triangulate, double each triangle to a parallelogram and count lattice points of its fundamental domain.
proofs.scope: All simple lattice polygons, convex or not. A triangle is a polygon with 3 vertices, and the induction on the number of vertices starts there.

roles.why: A simple polygon with more than 3 vertices has an interior diagonal, so it can be triangulated.
Lattice vertices make the cuts lattice segments and the point reflection preserve the lattice.

steps.slogan: Show that the defect $D=A-(I+\frac B2-1)$ is additive under cutting along a diagonal.
steps.detail: Cut $P$ along a diagonal with $c$ lattice points, endpoints included, into $P_1$ and $P_2$. Then $A=A_1+A_2$, $I=I_1+I_2+(c-2)$ and $B=B_1+B_2-2c+2$. Substitution gives $I+\frac B2-1=(I_1+\frac{B_1}2-1)+(I_2+\frac{B_2}2-1)$, so $D(P)=D(P_1)+D(P_2)$.

steps.slogan: Cut the polygon into lattice triangles along diagonals.
steps.detail: A simple polygon with more than 3 vertices has a diagonal inside it. Cutting along it gives two simple lattice polygons with fewer vertices. By induction on the number of vertices, $P$ is a union of lattice triangles glued along lattice diagonals, a [triangulation](c:polygon-triangulation).

steps.slogan: Double a lattice triangle into a lattice parallelogram by a point reflection.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be the midpoint of a side of a lattice triangle $T$, so $2M\in\mathbb{Z}^2$. The reflection $x\mapsto2M-x$ maps $\mathbb{Z}^2$ to itself, so the image $T'$ has the same $A,I,B$ and $D(T')=D(T)$. The parallelogram $\Pi=T\cup T'$ is cut along that side, so $D(\Pi)=2D(T)$ by step 1.

steps.slogan: Show $D=0$ for a lattice parallelogram by counting the points of a fundamental domain.
steps.detail: Let $\Pi$ be spanned by lattice vectors $u,v$ and put $N=|\det(u,v)|=A$. The sublattice $\mathbb{Z}u+\mathbb{Z}v$ has index $N$ in $\mathbb{Z}^2$, so the half-open parallelogram $\{su+tv:0\le s,t<1\}$ contains exactly $N$ lattice points, one per coset. They are the $I$ interior points and the $B/2-1$ boundary points on the two edges from the origin, far ends excluded, so $A=N=I+\frac B2-1$.

steps.slogan: Sum the defects of the triangles to get Pick's formula for $P$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $D(T)=0$ for every lattice triangle $T$. By step 2 and the additivity of step 1, $D(P)$ is the sum of the defects of the triangles, so $D(P)=0$, that is $A=I+\frac B2-1$.

concepts.c:simple-polygon: Simplicity gives interior diagonals and a well-defined interior and boundary.
concepts.c:lattice-point: Lattice points are counted, and lattice vertices keep every cut a lattice segment.
concepts.c:area: The area is compared with the point count through the defect.
concepts.c:polygon-triangulation: Triangulation reduces the formula to triangles.

source.note: The additivity, parallelogram and fundamental-domain proof, a standard proof of Pick's theorem.
